newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean refugee camp found empty as rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Zairean refugee camp found empty as rebels advance.

text.p: A U.N. team found on Thursday up to 55,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees missing from a camp in the jungle of eastern Zaire and advancing rebels denied any responsibility.
In diplomatic moves to prevent civil war from spilling further in Zaire, U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was due in South Africa to settle a date and venue for talks between the warring parties.

Not a single Rwandan refugee -- dead or alive -- remained visible at Kasese camp, 25 miles (15 km) south of Kisangani city. Last week bodies draped in blankets had been laid out in lines and many sick refugees were too weak to walk even one step.
"My impression was that the place was extremely sanitary for a camp where people had fled at a moment's notice," said Brenda Barton, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP).

"This is the first time a large group of refugees has disappeared on (rebel) alliance territory and the alliance is responsible to explain what happened to these people," said Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR.
A camp cholera hospital, which Friday had about 300 very sick patients, stood abandoned with bags for intravenous drips hanging from bamboo walls. The tents at the hospital had gone.
Overall there was very little debris when compared with other camps abandoned by refugees in their six-month exodus.
The Tutsi-dominated rebels sealed off the Kasese and Biaro camps south of Kisangani from aid workers and journalists on Monday, saying they were conducting a military operation.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda in the same year.

Rebels agreed to allow the U.N. mission to Kasese only after U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was appalled by the "inhumanity" of their action which he said was killing refugees by starvation.

"The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire...does not have a policy which consists in making life more difficult for the refugees," said Raphael N'genda, rebel "information minister".
He said France should let ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko use a supersonic Concorde airliner if he is too sick as he says to take a normal flight to talks in South Africa.

In Cape Town, South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said Sahnoun would return to South Africa to settle a date and a venue for direct talks and Mobutu and rebel Chief Laurent Kabila had reaffirmed their commitment to a negotiated peace.
Francois Lumumba, the son of Zaire's revered first prime minister Patrice Lumumba who was assassinated in 1961, surfaced in Geneva on Thursday to declare his support for the rebels.

"We congratulate Kabila and his forces for their courage in their armed struggle. We affirm our solidarity with the rebels. Their struggle is our struggle," Lumumba, 45, told a news conference, also attended by Zairean exiles in Switzerland.
The rebels said on Wednesday they had captured three gateway towns to Kinshasa and military analysts said guerrillas were in a position to choke off much of the capital's vital supplies.

"The rebel plan is becoming clearer now. They want to force the capital into submission, and the noose is tightening," said an analyst in Kinshasa after the rebels said they had seized Ilebo, Tshikapa and Dowete.

Rebel "justice minister" Mwenge Kongolo said he believed the fall of Kinshasa was a "matter of days rather than weeks". A military official in Kinshasa said it was possible rebels had taken Ilebo and Tshikapa.
Ilebo is Zaire's largest inland port and second most important after its only sea port at Matadi on the Atlantic.
In Matadi, the military governor of Lower Zaire Province appealed to local people to help the army defend the seaport.

Admiral Liwanga Mada took over formally as emergency rule administrator on Wednesday amid strong rumours that the rebels had infiltrated Matadi, which borders Angola. Security is tight in the city, which is full of SNIP military intelligence men.

The Angolan border is only five km (three miles) from Matadi and its government is said by regional analysts to be supportive of Kabila, who wants to topple Mobutu who for years backed Angola's UNITA rebels.
